Suppose you have measured a lot of things about a lot of objects and want to
look at the result. If you measured two things, you draw a scatter plot. If you
measured four, as in the data set on this page, you cannot draw the plot
anymore, and with recordings from hundreds of neurons the problem is far worse.
Principal component analysis (PCA) is the standard way out. It finds the few
directions in which the data actually vary and lets you look at those.

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Nothing needs installing, and the
figure updates as soon as you change a setting.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = "16px " + getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The data and the method

The data are the iris measurements collected by Anderson and made famous by
Fisher (1936), probably the most used data set in statistics: 150 flowers
from three species, and for each flower the length and width of a sepal and
of a petal, in centimetres. Nothing
about the method is specific to flowers. You could replace the four
measurements by the firing rates of four neurons and everything below would
read the same.

Write the measurements as a matrix $X$ with one row per flower and one column
per measurement, and subtract the mean of each column so that the cloud of
points is centred at the origin. The covariance matrix

$$C = \frac{1}{n} X^{\mathsf T} X$$

is a $4 \times 4$ table whose diagonal holds the variance of each measurement
and whose off-diagonal entries say how strongly two measurements vary together.
PCA, which goes back to Pearson (1901) and Hotelling (1933), asks a simple
question of this matrix: along which direction in the four-dimensional
measurement space is the spread of the data largest? The
answer is the eigenvector of $C$ with the largest eigenvalue,

$$C\, e_k = \lambda_k e_k ,$$

and the eigenvalue $\lambda_k$ is exactly the variance of the data along
$e_k$. The second principal component is the direction of largest spread
among all directions perpendicular to the first, and so on. Because the
eigenvalues add up to the total variance, the fraction
$\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j$ tells you how much of the data's variability
each component accounts for. If the first two fractions are large, a plot
along those two directions shows you most of what there is to see.

One detail matters more than it looks: whether you standardise. The
measurements all happen to be in centimetres here, but petal length ranges
over about six centimetres while sepal width ranges over barely two. Variance
grows with the square of the range, so without any correction the first
component is mostly petal length, simply because that number is the biggest.
Dividing each column by its standard deviation puts all four measurements on
an equal footing. Whether that is the right thing to do depends on the data.
If the measurements have different units, you almost always want it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
irisRaw = FileAttachment("iris.json").json()
viewof pcStd = Inputs.toggle({label: "Standardise each variable (z-score)", value: true})
pcAxisOpts = new Map([["PC 1", "pc0"], ["PC 2", "pc1"], ["PC 3", "pc2"], ["PC 4", "pc3"],
  ...irisRaw.features.map((f, i) => [f, "v" + i])])
viewof pcX = Inputs.select(pcAxisOpts, {value: "pc0", label: "Horizontal axis"})
viewof pcY = Inputs.select(pcAxisOpts, {value: "pc1", label: "Vertical axis"})
viewof pcColour = Inputs.toggle({label: "Colour by species", value: true})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
symEig = A => {           // Jacobi eigenvalue iteration for a small symmetric matrix
  const n = A.length, a = A.map(r => r.slice()), v = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => Array.from({length: n}, (_, j) => +(i === j)));
  for (let sweep = 0; sweep < 60; sweep++) {
    let off = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) off += a[i][j] ** 2;
    if (off < 1e-18) break;
    for (let p = 0; p < n; p++) for (let q = p + 1; q < n; q++) {
      if (Math.abs(a[p][q]) < 1e-15) continue;
      const th = (a[q][q] - a[p][p]) / (2 * a[p][q]), t = Math.sign(th || 1) / (Math.abs(th) + Math.sqrt(th * th + 1));
      const cs = 1 / Math.sqrt(t * t + 1), sn = t * cs;
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const akp = a[k][p], akq = a[k][q]; a[k][p] = cs * akp - sn * akq; a[k][q] = sn * akp + cs * akq; }
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const apk = a[p][k], aqk = a[q][k]; a[p][k] = cs * apk - sn * aqk; a[q][k] = sn * apk + cs * aqk; }
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const vkp = v[k][p], vkq = v[k][q]; v[k][p] = cs * vkp - sn * vkq; v[k][q] = sn * vkp + cs * vkq; }
    }
  }
  const order = [...Array(n).keys()].sort((i, j) => a[j][j] - a[i][i]);
  return {values: order.map(i => a[i][i]), vectors: order.map(i => { const col = v.map(r => r[i]); const big = col.reduce((b, x) => Math.abs(x) > Math.abs(b) ? x : b, 0); return big < 0 ? col.map(x => -x) : col; })};
}
pca = {
  const rows = irisRaw.rows, d = 4, n = rows.length;
  const mean = Array.from({length: d}, (_, j) => rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r[j], 0) / n);
  const sd = Array.from({length: d}, (_, j) => Math.sqrt(rows.reduce((s, r) => s + (r[j] - mean[j]) ** 2, 0) / n));
  const X = rows.map(r => Array.from({length: d}, (_, j) => (r[j] - mean[j]) / (pcStd ? sd[j] : 1)));
  const C = Array.from({length: d}, (_, i) => Array.from({length: d}, (_, j) => X.reduce((s, x) => s + x[i] * x[j], 0) / n));
  const {values, vectors} = symEig(C);
  const scores = X.map(x => vectors.map(e => e.reduce((s, ei, j) => s + ei * x[j], 0)));
  const total = values.reduce((s, l) => s + l, 0);
  return {X, C, values, vectors, scores, total, species: rows.map(r => r[4]), mean, sd};
}
pcCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 580)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const c = pcCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 580, cols = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c"];
  const {X, values, vectors, scores, total, species} = pca, feats = irisRaw.features;
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  const get = (key, i) => key.startsWith("pc") ? scores[i][+key[2]] : X[i][+key[1]];
  const label = key => key.startsWith("pc") ? `PC ${+key[2] + 1}` : feats[+key[1]] + (pcStd ? " (z-scored)" : " (cm, centred)");
  const xs = X.map((_, i) => get(pcX, i)), ys = X.map((_, i) => get(pcY, i));
  const lim = Math.max(...xs.map(Math.abs), ...ys.map(Math.abs)) * 1.1;
  const sP = {x0: 90, y0: 12, s: 360};
  const px = v => sP.x0 + sP.s * (v + lim) / (2 * lim), py = v => sP.y0 + sP.s * (1 - (v + lim) / (2 * lim));
  axisBox(c, sP.x0, sP.y0, sP.s, sP.s);
  c.strokeStyle = "#ccc"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(px(0), sP.y0); c.lineTo(px(0), sP.y0 + sP.s); c.moveTo(sP.x0, py(0)); c.lineTo(sP.x0 + sP.s, py(0)); c.stroke();
  // principal axes drawn in the plane of two raw variables
  if (!pcX.startsWith("pc") && !pcY.startsWith("pc")) {
    const i = +pcX[1], j = +pcY[1];
    for (const [k, col] of [[0, "#d62728"], [1, "#9467bd"]]) {
      const e = vectors[k], L = 2 * Math.sqrt(values[k]);
      c.strokeStyle = col; c.lineWidth = 3; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(px(-L * e[i]), py(-L * e[j])); c.lineTo(px(L * e[i]), py(L * e[j])); c.stroke();
      c.fillStyle = col; c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(`PC ${k + 1}`, px(L * e[i]) + 6, py(L * e[j]) + 5);
    }
  }
  X.forEach((_, i) => { c.fillStyle = pcColour ? cols[species[i]] : "#555"; c.globalAlpha = 0.6; c.beginPath(); c.arc(px(xs[i]), py(ys[i]), 4.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); });
  c.globalAlpha = 1; c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText(label(pcX), sP.x0 + sP.s / 2, sP.y0 + sP.s + 24);
  c.fillText((-lim).toFixed(1), sP.x0, sP.y0 + sP.s + 44); c.fillText(lim.toFixed(1), sP.x0 + sP.s, sP.y0 + sP.s + 44);
  c.save(); c.translate(sP.x0 - 60, sP.y0 + sP.s / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.fillText(label(pcY), 0, 0); c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText(lim.toFixed(1), sP.x0 - 8, sP.y0 + 6); c.fillText((-lim).toFixed(1), sP.x0 - 8, sP.y0 + sP.s + 2);
  if (pcColour) irisRaw.species.forEach((s, k) => { c.fillStyle = cols[k]; c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(s, sP.x0 + 10, sP.y0 + 22 + 22 * k); });
  // explained variance bars, right
  const bP = {x0: 520, y0: 12, w: 220, h: 150};
  axisBox(c, bP.x0, bP.y0, bP.w, bP.h);
  values.forEach((l, k) => {
    const frac = l / total, bw = bP.w / 4 * 0.7, bx = bP.x0 + bP.w * (k + 0.15) / 4;
    c.fillStyle = "#1f77b4"; c.fillRect(bx, bP.y0 + bP.h * (1 - frac), bw, bP.h * frac);
    c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`${(100 * frac).toFixed(0)}%`, bx + bw / 2, bP.y0 + bP.h * (1 - frac) - 6);
    c.fillText(`PC ${k + 1}`, bx + bw / 2, bP.y0 + bP.h + 22);
  });
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("explained variance", bP.x0 + bP.w / 2, bP.y0 + bP.h + 44);
  // loadings table, full width below the scatter
  const tY = 470, colX = j => 250 + 125 * j;
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText("loadings: components of each eₖ", 90, tY);
  c.font = "14px " + getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily;
  feats.forEach((f, j) => { c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(f, colX(j), tY + 24); });
  values.forEach((_, k) => {
    c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(`PC ${k + 1}`, 90, tY + 46 + 20 * k);
    vectors[k].forEach((e, j) => { c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(e.toFixed(2), colX(j), tY + 46 + 20 * k); });
  });
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The large panel on the left is the scatter plot. Each dot is one flower,
placed according to whatever you chose for the two axes. By default these are
the first two principal components, so you are looking at the
four-dimensional cloud from the angle that shows the most spread. Colour marks
the species, blue for *setosa*, orange for *versicolor* and green for
*virginica*. It is worth switching the colours off for a moment: the grey
cloud is what PCA actually works with. The method never sees the species
labels, and yet the three groups come out separated, because the differences
between species are also the biggest source of variance in the data.

You can also put two of the original measurements on the axes. Then the plot
is an ordinary scatter plot of those two columns, and on top of it the first
two principal components are drawn as lines through the origin, PC 1 in red
and PC 2 in purple. Each line is as long as two standard deviations of the
data along it, so you see both where the component points and how much of the
spread it captures. Note that the lines are projections of four-dimensional
directions onto the two measurements you picked, so they need not look
perpendicular.

The bars on the right show the share of the total variance that each
component explains. With standardisation on, the first component accounts for
roughly three quarters and the second for most of the rest, which is the
justification for looking at only two of the four dimensions. Below the
scatter plot is the table of loadings, the entries of each eigenvector. A
loading says how much a given measurement contributes to a component. The
first component has similar loadings on three of the four measurements with
the same sign, so it is essentially "overall size of the flower". The second
is dominated by sepal width and separates flowers that are wide for their size
from those that are narrow.

## Things to try

Switch standardisation off and watch the loadings table. The first component
is now almost entirely petal length, and the explained-variance share of PC 1
goes up, not because the structure got cleaner but because one variable with
a large range now dominates. Then put petal length and sepal width on the two
axes, with standardisation still off, and look at where the red line points.

Put the third and fourth components on the axes. There is almost nothing left
to see, which is what a small eigenvalue means in practice: those directions
are mostly measurement noise and natural variation within a species.

This page is based on the dimensionality-reduction exercise in Dayan and
Abbott (2001). For how the same method is used on neural population
recordings, where the "measurements" are the firing rates of many neurons,
Cunningham and Yu (2014) is a good starting point.

## References

Cunningham JP, Yu BM (2014). Dimensionality reduction for large-scale neural
recordings. *Nature Neuroscience* 17: 1500–1509.

Dayan P, Abbott LF (2001). *Theoretical Neuroscience: Computational and
Mathematical Modeling of Neural Systems*. MIT Press.

Fisher RA (1936). The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems.
*Annals of Eugenics* 7: 179–188.

Hotelling H (1933). Analysis of a complex of statistical variables into
principal components. *Journal of Educational Psychology* 24: 417–441.

Pearson K (1901). On lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in
space. *Philosophical Magazine* 2: 559–572.
